class.name: NetwRateWindow
class.brief_description: A per-peer sliding rate window: how many requests of one kind a peer may make inside a span, and who is exempt from asking.
class.description: The window slides rather than resetting, which is the property that separates a flood guard from a throttle. A peer asking steadily under [member limit] is never refused however long it keeps going, and a peer that spent its budget is admitted again the moment its oldest request ages out of [member span_msec]. [method exceeded] takes the clock instead of reading it, and that is what makes the span testable at all: a wall clock cannot be asked to be a second past itself. Callers read [method Time.get_ticks_msec] and hand it down. [codeblock] limit 8, span_msec 1000 8 requests at t=0 admitted the 9th at t=0 REFUSED the 9th at t=1001 admitted, because the first eight aged out one request every 200 ms admitted forever, since five per second is under eight [/codeblock] One rule with more than one consumer. A session admits joins under it and a scene column admits change requests under it, so a peer that cannot flood one cannot flood the other by a different route.

method.name: clear
method.description: Forgets every peer's spend. A session teardown calls it, so a returning peer is not held to the budget a previous session spent on its behalf.

method.name: exceeded
method.description: Records one request from [param peer_id] at [param now_msec] and returns whether it exceeded [member limit], counting the one just recorded. A [param peer_id] equal to [member exempt_peer] is never counted and always returns [code]false[/code].

members.member: The one peer the window never counts. Server authority asks itself for things, and a host that could flood itself out of its own session is a guard working against the peer it exists to protect. Set it to a peer id nobody holds to exempt no one.
How many requests one peer may make inside [member span_msec]. The default is chosen so an honest peer that asks once, and twice at most through a resend path, stays far under it.
How long a recorded request counts against its peer.

The size the table may reach before peers whose newest request already aged out are dropped from it, so a long-lived server never accumulates every peer it ever saw. The prune never drops the peer whose request triggered it.
